fixes.explanation: Idols aren't in this verse at all. Paul's appeal is about how the believers treat each other. He says he wants "…no divisions among you…" and wants them "…united in mind and conviction." (1 Corinthians 1:10) So the missing word is divisions.

True. Paul says, "…some from Chloe’s household have informed me that there are quarrels among you." (1 Corinthians 1:11) He says who told him, too: some from Chloe's household. The news made it all the way to him, and he's got a response ready.

Christ it is. Paul lists the four lines people are saying: "I follow Paul…" "I follow Apollos…" "I follow Cephas…" or "I follow Christ." (1 Corinthians 1:12) Notice Christ's name comes last on that list. Paul says this is what he means by the quarrels, and I'm not going to add a reason he doesn't give.
John isn't one of the names in this list. The four lines Paul gives are Paul, Apollos, Cephas and Christ. (1 Corinthians 1:12) The fourth one is the answer you're hunting for.

Not quite, friend. Paul asks, "Was Paul crucified for you?" (1 Corinthians 1:13) He's putting his own name next to Christ's to show how silly the comparison is. The answer he's after is no, so this one is False. Paul wasn't crucified for them, and he knows it.

Build a church for Paul? That's a big construction project, and he never brings it up. His question is, "Were you baptized into the name of Paul?" (1 Corinthians 1:13) It's all about whose name they were baptized into.

All of them would be a LONG list, and Paul is glad his is short. He says, "I thank God that I did not baptize any of you except Crispus and Gaius…" (1 Corinthians 1:14) Two names, and then he adds the household of Stephanas. (1 Corinthians 1:16) Nobody could call that all of them.

Jerusalem isn't mentioned in this verse, friend. Paul says, "…Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel…" (1 Corinthians 1:17) Leading a church in Jerusalem would be a big job, but it isn't the one Paul names.

Yes. Paul says Christ sent him to preach the gospel "…not with words of wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power." (1 Corinthians 1:17) He's worried about the cross being emptied of its power, friend. That's the reason he gives for skipping the fancy words.

A riddle is a nice guess, friend, but it's not Paul's word. He writes, "…the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing…" (1 Corinthians 1:18) A riddle is something you puzzle over. Paul's word is foolishness.

True. Paul asks, "Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?" (1 Corinthians 1:20) He asks it right after, "Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the philosopher of this age?" Those questions all lead up to it.

Through what was preached, yes. Paul writes, "…God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe." (1 Corinthians 1:21) That's the way God was pleased to save those who believe, since the world through its wisdom did not know Him. And to those who are called, Paul says Christ is "…the power of God and the wisdom of God." (1 Corinthians 1:24)

Priests aren't in this verse, friend, and I checked twice. Paul says, "…God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe." (1 Corinthians 1:21) The way he names is the preaching.

Kings? No throne room in this verse, friend. Paul says, "…God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe." (1 Corinthians 1:21) The way he points to is the preaching, and nobody had to be crowned for it.

Stumbling block. Paul says Christ crucified is "…a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles…" (1 Corinthians 1:23) Picture a toe finding the one chair leg in a dark kitchen. For Jews, that's what Paul says Christ crucified is, something to trip over.

False. Paul says "…to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God." (1 Corinthians 1:24) Jews and Greeks are both in the called. Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God to those who are called.
Stronger. Paul says, "…the weakness of God is stronger than man’s strength." (1 Corinthians 1:25) Think about that for a second. Paul pairs it with God's foolishness being wiser than man's wisdom.
Teach is a gentle word, friend, and I like it, but it's not the word Paul picked. He says, "…God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise…" (1 Corinthians 1:27) The text says shame.

Honor would be quite the plot twist for the wise, friend, but the verse goes the other way. Paul writes, "…God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise…" (1 Corinthians 1:27) God chose them to shame the wise, not to honor them.

The world copying His ways? Nice thought, friend, but Paul doesn't go there. He says God chose them "…so that no one may boast in His presence." (1 Corinthians 1:29) The reason he gives is about boasting, not copying.
Law isn't in this verse, friend. Paul says, "Let him who boasts boast in the Lord." (1 Corinthians 1:31) The Lord is who gets the credit. Not the law, and not Paul, Apollos or Cephas either.
